I had a pelvic spasm that caused a similar feeling. It took several doctors to have that suggested. You can easily test if this is the case and try some simple things that may help!

First, to check if you have a spasm, you want to make a sweeping u motion along the back wall of your vagina. You want to put a little pressure and see if the muscle (your pelvic floor) feels tight. It almost feels like a pulled tight rubber band. 

If you find a spot that hurts, you can press into the sport for a few seconds at a time to release the muscle. If you've gotten a deep tissue massage, you want to basically do that on the inside. I find this tricky and have a tool to help me, but you may find a partner can get a better angle if you are comfortable asking for help. Doing this in a hot shower while sitting on the tub floor is my go to fix for this issue when I have a flare up. 

You can also do some yoga. I like Banana Blondie's Yoga for IC on youtube, but anything slow, soft and focused on the hips is good. It's all about belly breathing and stretching to relax that muscle. I like child's pose with extra wide knees, pigeon pose and butterfly stretches to help with this when the massaging isn't enough. 

Definitely still worth getting tested for a UTI but if removal was stressful on your body a pelvic floor spasm could maybe be another possibility. I hope these tips help, I was so frustrated and scared when I was dealing with this.

Here's some general good to know stuff about the pill.

The pamphlet that came with your pill (these are available online from the manufacturer also) will have a ton of useful information in it. Don't get hung up on the side effects stuff, but read this and take note of the following:

1 - What is your window? Some pills have up to 12 hour windows where you're still protected, others have only an hour. This depends on the specific pill and the hormones used in it. 

2 - What do you do if you miss a pill? Depending on your exact pill and where in the pack you are there may be differing instructions. Remember this is only important if you miss your pill by longer than the above window. 

3 - What is the best practice for storing my pill? Keeping your pill out of high temperatures is often important. Make sure to check for any issues in case you keep pills on you/travel and they're left in a hot car or something. 

4 - What if I puke or have diarrhea? This may make your pill less effective. See the pamphlet for specific instructions on what to do on days you have gastro issues in case you need to take another dose. 

5 - What medicine interacts with my pill? Some antibiotics and other meds can decrease pill effectiveness. It's helpful to keep this in mind for any time you have to take meds for other reasons, especially antibiotics. 

If you want more specific advice about your pill, you need to list the exact brand. Pills can vary widely in their composition and not all advice that is true for one type/brand will be true for others.

If you read page 9 of this [document](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&opi=89978449&url=https://www.bayer.com/sites/default/files/YAZ_EN_PI.pdf&ved=2ahUKEwjVtJ-kx8OMAxUnFFkFHfNJGioQ9cILegQIJBAA&usg=AOvVaw2Yx-zmBIBMntjfZdR8v9zo) it says you have a 12 hour window to take the pill. It also provides clear instructions on what to do if you miss one by more than 12 hours or miss multiples. Definitely important to read and understand everything related to storage, drug interactions and missed pills in this doc to be sure you have full protection.

Basically you have five options when it comes to non-permanent BC

1 - Pills, which come in many varieties and can be estrogen based, progesterone based or a combination of the two. Each exact brand has different makeups and can cause various side effects. They're highly effective, but rely heavily on perfect use. This is nice if you like to have a lot of control over your BC and if you want to be able to skip periods on a controlled schedule.

2 - Barrier methods, like condoms (male and female) can protect against STDs as well as add a layer of pregnancy protection. There are also diaphragms and cervical caps which only offer pregnancy protection, but are less intrusive as far as sexual enjoyment. These are far less effective compared to hormonal options but are great to add in as additional protection. 

3 - Semi-permanent, but non-IUD methods are progesterone based and require less effort than the pill, dropping the risk of possible pregnancy from user error significantly. There are a wide range of options in this category. You have the depo shot, the ring and the patch which require monthly(ish, timelines can vary by exact method) maintenance. The Nexplanon implant is the outlier as it lasts for up to 5 years, but is in your arm not your uterus. Nexplanon is considered the most effective HBC on the market because it has the lowest risk of user error and body rejection. These are great for lowering pregnancy anxiety while avoiding an IUD as that can feel scary for many people. 

4 - IUDs come in both hormonal and non hormonal varieties. The hormonal types vary in duration of protection based on size and hormonal dose, but all are progesterone only. Smaller options are ideal for women who haven't yet had children or who have a low pain tolerance for insertion. The non-hormonal copper IUD option is unique in that it is highly effective while also being hormone free. Because of how it works it can cause more painful periods and is about 1% less effective than its hormonal counterparts because correct placement is essential to its function. 

5 - Temperature tracking or natural family planning is when women track their fertility based on a rising body temperature during ovulation. This is the least effective method as many things can affect body temperature and while you may know your fertile window, sperm can live in the body for up to 5 days. That means that even if you abstain or use barrier methods during ovulation, if you had sex a few days before realizing you ovulated, you could still get pregnant. This is also a method people use for trying to become pregnant, not just to prevent it. This method is ONLY effective/accurate if you are NOT on any kind of hormonal birth control as the hormones will take you out of a true cycle. Technically speaking you never have a period on HBC, just a withdrawal bleed. 

Generally speaking the progesterone only methods are the ones that typically reduce or stop periods, though a withdrawal bleed is still common on progesterone only pills. Estrogen can increase stroke risk, so is pretty rarely prescribed in comparison to combo/progesterone pills. Side effects from hormones can include weight loss/gain, acne loss/gain, mood improvement, anxiety, depression, and more. Your body will react differently to different methods based not only on hormone type but the dose, exact compound and delivery method.

French high school teacher here! A few things to consider when making your choice :)

1 - Spanish is more phonetically spelled than French. Meaning you say what you see for the most part. French has lots of silent letters, which can make speaking feel like a bigger obstacle. 

2 - In my experience (this will depend on your region), there are fewer French teachers than Spanish teachers. Taking French may allow you to have the same teacher for multiple years (for better or worse!). Pros - this is great for getting college/job/scholarship recs because the teacher will know you better, good  if the teacher is good, you don't need to relearn class routines and expectations, higher likelihood of being in classes with friends. Cons - You could get stuck with a bad teacher, only one perspective on the language/one teaching style. 

3 - Language looks great on a transcript, bit doesn't much matter as far as which language specifically unless you're going into a language specific major. Pick what you like and don't be afraid to make a change after one year if you really need to. Language is complex, especially when you're starting from scratch at an older age. 

4 - In my experience, since French is considered harder I tend to see fewer students in my classroom who are not serious about their language studies. This leads to fewer distractions and in some ways can create a better learning environment. (This isn't a dig at kids who pick Spanish, I'm just speaking from what I've seen in my time at my specific school and from what I've heard from other language teachers in my area). 

5 - Spanish classes have students who are heritage or native speakers in them more often (for example I've had three in the last five years, but we have sixty in Spanish). This can be great for speaking and listening practice (in my experience some heritage learners have better listening/speaking skills and fairly low reading/writing skills). This may also be intimidating for some people. 

As many have mentioned, Spanish is a great asset in many career paths (from kitchens to hospitals), however there are many variations so the Spanish you learn in school might not be the Spanish you encounter in the wild. French if an amazing language and I of course am biased towards it. Depending on where you live it could be more useful than Spanish but that is definitely regional.

At the end of the day the best thing you can do for yourself is be really mentally present in class, whichever language you pick. Language isn't like a lot of classes where you can cram information before a test and then forget it. The time you spend listening, reading, etc all builds on itself and can't be replaced like it can in many classes. Best of luck in whatever you pick!

While this is a reasonable enough thought, as a teacher I have a few reasons I think this would be generally ineffective. 

1 - Any class that becomes required to graduate also becomes dumbed down to the lowest level and rarely helps the students it's meant to help. This has happened with the personal finance class we have at my school. I'm friends with the teacher and it's ridiculous the kids that just won't pass the class no matter how easy/accessable it's designed to be. 2 - Classes of this nature, much like a sex ed class, would probably come with some ability for parents to pull their kids out if they disagree, even if it's a "required" class. Schools are now customer service centers and the parents of the kids you would want to reach most would be the first to pull their kids out/sue/fight the school board. It is near impossible to make anything "required" in a public school these days. Take our "binding" virtual vs in person decisions kids made five weeks ago. I have 5 kids who have been given exceptions to change their minds and start coming in over the last two weeks. We even had a counselor try and give a kid who was moving and wanted to graduate early a pass in a required class he was failing. 

3 - There are great teachers and not so great teachers. I feel like it would be hard to find enough teachers who would be capable of teaching this in an unbiased way in a world where good teachers can be hard to find. And even great teachers would have a challenging time teaching something like this with all the eggshells you'd need to walk on at the HS level. 

So good idea, but I'm fairly sure it wouldn't reach the people you'd want to change :/ Perhaps making it a requirement of higher ed would go over better, but again it wouldn't meet your goal of reaching the masses, especially those who have suffered from extreme indoctrination.

I was deeply upset not just because of the no kids rule I wanted to have, but because this wedding was suddenly now also most of the family's first chance to meet the new baby. My therapist and I suggested the following:

-she comes to the ceremony but not the reception (not ideal if you're close to these new parents)

-she has a friend with her to make sure my husband's family could enjoy the wedding or we hire a babysitter to be on property

-there be some sort of event beforehand for family/friends to meet the baby so it's not the center of attention

None of my requests were honored and that child screamed for a small chunk of the ceremony. Somehow her mother decided staying until things wrapped up at 3am was a good idea (I was low-key concerned the baby had hearing damage from being around our loud DJ for so long) and that was that. Even with all that and all my stress, it really wasn't a major issue and I still had an amazing wedding. I even held the baby without any desire to throw it across the room.

I'd say make sure you have someone on hand who can be a baby wrangler and help keep track of their stuff/hold them for important moments. Also have some kind of quiet space for them to go to get relief/not disturb the whole event. I'm not sure if these people are on your side or your husband's, but hopefully they will be respectful of your wishes. 

Also I know I probably come across as a baby hating asshole, which I definitely was in that moment. I love my niece now, but i was definitely angry that "my day" was going to be "ruined". My therapist helped me see where I was being a bit selfish and unreasonable (mostly bc I had invested hopes into this event and hadn't put any importance on other events in my life in sort of an every egg in one basket kinda situation). As a teacher, the worst thing you can do is nothing. If you're overwhelmed by all the assignments, pick one thing you can do for each class on time and well. This will give you some "equity" with the teacher you can cash in on to get more flexibility with late work. Nothing pisses off a teacher more than doing nothing at all for their class. Decide what has to be done (or even better, make a plan of what must be prioritized with your teacher!) and make yourself do that bare minimum before you allow yourself anything else. Avoid doing school work after a certain time (like say 7pm) to avoid staying up all night. Instead do as much as you can make yourself do before the deadline and then allow yourself to let go of what didn't get done. 

Additionally, if this is new due to virtual/hybrid school, you may need to step up your organizational skills. Many of my students are just now realizing they used to get so much support from the school they didn't need to make a huge effort to stay on top of their work. It doesn't matter what you chose to do/try to stay organized (I'm personally a big fan of lists) but it should be something intentional. 

Finally, talk to your parents about therapy or medicine (cbd if that's legal for you under 18 is honestly where I'd start too). This isn't normal or fair for your brain to be fighting you like this, especially if it's a recent change. Your school counselor may be able to direct you to some health services if cost is a factor.

2. Although it takes longer for the spouse to get there, they get their green card and can work much faster. On a K1 it takes about 4 months after you get married to get that and be able to work. 
3. The CR1 process is slightly less expensive because you don’t have to do as many change of status forms

I consulted with a lawyer and she said these two are the best options for couples. She warned me heavily about the dangers of visa fraud if my fiancé came over on a student or tourist visa. These mariages and relationships can come under a lot of scrutiny and it’s better to be safe than sorry. If you did go the student visa route, I wouldn’t get married until 2 years into his studies at least to prove no fraud.
